questions.question: What are generics in Java and why are they used?
questions.title: Java Generics Basics
questions.direct_answer: Generics provide compile-time type safety for collections and classes, eliminating ClassCastException at runtime by catching type mismatches at compile time.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that generics are erased at runtime (type erasure) — generic type info is not available via reflection
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain type erasure and bounded wildcards (<? extends T> vs <? super T>)

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So generics let you write classes and methods that work with any type while still getting compile-time type checking. Before generics (Java 1.4), a List held Objects and you had to cast everything manually — which meant ClassCastException errors at runtime.

With generics: `List<String> names` tells the compiler this list only holds Strings. Try to add an Integer and the code won't compile. No casting needed when getting elements out.

The T in `class Box<T>` is a type parameter. When you write `Box<String>`, T becomes String throughout the class.

Type erasure: generics are a compile-time feature only. At runtime, `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` are both just `List`. The type parameter is erased. This means you can't do `new T[]` or `instanceof List<String>` — only `instanceof List`.

Bounded wildcards: `<? extends T>` means 'some type that is T or a subtype' — read-only (upper bound). `<? super T>` means 'some type that is T or a supertype' — write-only (lower bound). The PECS rule: Producer Extends, Consumer Super.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Compile-time type safety — catches ClassCastException before runtime
Type erasure: generics info removed at runtime
<? extends T> = wildcard for reading (upper bound)
<? super T> = wildcard for writing (lower bound)

speakable_v2.hook: Generics move type errors from a runtime crash to a compile-time warning — that's a free bug fix before you even run the code.

beats.text: Generics let you write classes and methods that work with any type while the compiler enforces type safety. You parameterize a class with a type placeholder like T. Before generics (Java 1.4), List held Object and you needed manual casts everywhere — any mismatch was a ClassCastException at runtime. With generics, List only accepts Strings, and wrong types are compile errors.

Generics exist to catch type mismatches at compile time rather than runtime. They also eliminate the need for explicit casting when reading from collections, making code cleaner and safer without any runtime overhead.

items: Type parameter T: a placeholder replaced with a real type at use time — List becomes List when you write List.
Bounded type parameter: T extends Number limits T to Number and its subtypes — useful for numeric operations.
Type erasure: at runtime all generic type info is removed — List and List are both just List on the JVM.

beats.text: sharp edge: type erasure means you can't write new T[] or check instanceof List — the JVM has no record of T at runtime. In the product catalog app, List productList is type-safe at compile time, but the JVM sees just a plain List. This is why generic array creation fails — the JVM can't enforce the element type at runtime.

items: Don't try instanceof List — it won't compile because the type parameter is erased at runtime. Use instanceof List instead.
Avoid raw types like List without a type parameter — they bypass all compile-time checking and can introduce hidden ClassCastExceptions.

speakable_v2.cap: Generics give you compile-time type safety for free — use them everywhere and never use raw types in new code.

questions.question: What are bounded wildcards in Java generics and when do you use them?
questions.title: Bounded Wildcards
questions.direct_answer: <? extends T> means a subtype of T (read-only use); <? super T> means a supertype of T (write-friendly use) — the PECS rule guides the choice.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Trying to add to a <? extends T> collection (compiler forbids it)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain PECS with a concrete Collections.copy() example

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So Java generics wildcards are for writing methods that work with collections of multiple types.

`<? extends T>` means 'a collection of some type that is T or a subtype.' You can read T objects from it, but you can't add to it because the compiler doesn't know the exact type. Use this when the collection is a producer (you read from it).

`<? super T>` means 'a collection of some type that is T or a supertype.' You can add T objects to it (since T is a subtype), but reading gives you Object. Use when the collection is a consumer (you write to it).

The PECS rule: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. Example: `Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)` — src produces values (extends), dest consumes them (super).

followup_questions: Why can't you add to a List<? extends Number>?

seo.metaTitle: Java Generics Bounded Wildcards — extends vs super
seo.metaDescription: Bounded wildcards in Java generics — extends for reading, super for writing, and the PECS rule.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app storing a list of products and looking them up by ID
familiarity_anchors: a read-only folder vs a write-only inbox
a supplier vs a consumer in a factory
speakable_v2.hook: Extends means you can read from it; super means you can write to it — PECS keeps it straight.

groups.heading: ? extends T (upper bound)
groups.text: Means the collection holds some type that is T or a subtype. You can read T objects out of it safely. You can't add to it — the compiler doesn't know the exact subtype, so adding anything would be unsafe.

groups.heading: ? super T (lower bound)
groups.text: Means the collection holds some type that is T or a supertype. You can add T objects into it safely (T is always a valid subtype). Reading gives you Object, not T, because you don't know the exact supertype.

items: Use ? extends T when your method only reads from the collection (producer) — like summing a list of numbers.
Use ? super T when your method only writes to the collection (consumer) — like filling a destination list.
The PECS rule: Producer Extends, Consumer Super — Collections.copy(dest super T, src extends T) is the textbook example.

beats.text: candidates miss: trying to add to a List — the compiler rejects it because the list could be a List or List and adding any element could violate type safety. This confuses many freshers who expect extends to mean 'I can add subtypes'.

speakable_v2.cap: PECS: use extends when you're only reading, super when you're only writing — and when both, use the exact type parameter T.

questions.question: How do you write a generic class and a generic method in Java?
questions.title: Generic Classes and Methods
questions.direct_answer: Generic class: class Box<T> { T value; }. Generic method: <T> T getFirst(List<T> list) { return list.get(0); } — the type parameter goes before the return type.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Putting type parameter in wrong place for generic methods, or using raw types
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show a generic swap method and explain that type inference means you usually don't need to specify <T> explicitly

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content:
So a generic class declares the type parameter after the class name: `class Pair<A, B>`. Inside, you use A and B as type placeholders. Users specify the types when creating instances: `new Pair<String, Integer>("age", 25)`.

A generic method declares its type parameter before the return type: `public <T> T getFirst(List<T> list)`. The type parameter is inferred from the argument at the call site — you write `getFirst(myStringList)` and Java infers T=String. You rarely need to write `this.<String>getFirst(list)` explicitly.

A common generic utility method: swap two elements in a list. `public static <T> void swap(List<T> list, int i, int j)` — works for any List type without casting.

seo.metaTitle: Generic Class and Generic Method in Java
seo.metaDescription: How to write generic classes and methods in Java — syntax, type inference, and practical examples.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app storing a list of products and looking them up by ID
familiarity_anchors: a template with a blank to fill in
a function that works on any type
a reusable container with a type label
speakable_v2.hook: Generic class: put T after the class name. Generic method: put T before the return type — that's the whole syntax.

beats.text: A generic class declares type parameters after the class name in angle brackets: class Box has a type parameter T used throughout the class. A generic method declares its type parameter before the return type: public T getFirst(List list). The compiler infers T from what you pass in, so you rarely need to specify it explicitly.

Generic classes and methods let you write reusable, type-safe code without duplication. Instead of writing a swap method for every possible type, one generic swap works for List, List, and anything else.

items: Generic class syntax: class Pair — declare T after the class name, then use T as a type anywhere inside.
Generic method syntax: public static T swap(List list, int i, int j) — T declared before the return type.
Type inference: when you call getFirst(myProductList), Java infers T = Product automatically — no explicit T needed.

beats.text: non-obvious: a generic method can appear in a non-generic class. You don't need the class to be parameterized to write a generic utility method — static utility methods like Collections.swap are a good example of this pattern.

items: Don't put the type parameter after the return type — it goes before it. public T T getFirst() is wrong; public T getFirst() is correct.
Avoid raw types like List list without a parameter — the compiler won't warn about type errors and you lose the safety generics provide.

speakable_v2.cap: Generic syntax is mostly angle brackets in the right place — and type inference means you usually don't have to spell out the type at the call site.

questions.question: What are raw types and why should you avoid them?
questions.title: Raw Types
questions.direct_answer: A raw type is a generic class used without its type parameter (e.g., List instead of List<String>) — it disables compile-time type checking and can cause runtime ClassCastException.

interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using raw types in new code because 'it compiles' without warnings enabled
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that raw types exist only for backward compatibility with pre-Java-5 code

sections.title: Key Points
content: Raw type: List, Map instead of List<String>, Map<K,V>
Only valid use: legacy code interoperability with pre-Java-5 APIs

followup_questions: What warning does Java give for raw types?
When is using raw types acceptable?

seo.metaTitle: Java Raw Types — What They Are and Why to Avoid Them
seo.metaDescription: Raw types in Java generics — what they are, runtime risks, and why to always use parameterized types.

speakable_v2.standard_example: Java 17 app storing a list of products and looking them up by ID
familiarity_anchors: a unlabeled box that accepts anything
turning off safety guards on a machine
speakable_v2.hook: A raw type silently turns off the type safety you paid for with generics — and the compiler lets it happen without an error.

beats.text: A raw type is a generic class used without its type parameter — writing List instead of List or Map instead of Map. The compiler treats it as holding Object, strips all generic type checking, and issues 'unchecked' warnings. You're back to pre-Java-5 behavior where any type mismatch becomes a ClassCastException at runtime.

Raw types exist solely for backward compatibility. Before Java 5 introduced generics, all collections held Object. Java kept raw types valid so old code still compiles. There's no legitimate reason to use them in new code.

items: Raw type: List, Map, Set — no angle brackets.
Effect: compiler treats all elements as Object — no add type check, no get type inference.
Risk: ClassCastException at runtime when you retrieve and cast an element to the wrong type.
Warning: the compiler emits 'unchecked' warnings — treat these as errors in modern code.

beats.text: production trap: a raw List in a product catalog service quietly accepts both String and Product objects. The code compiles cleanly (with suppressed warnings), but retrieving an element and casting it to Product throws ClassCastException on the String entries — a runtime crash in production that should have been a compile error.

items: Never suppress unchecked warnings without understanding them — they're the compiler telling you raw types are present.
The one acceptable use: interfacing with legacy pre-Java-5 APIs you can't change. In all other cases, always parameterize.

speakable_v2.cap: Raw types exist for backward compatibility only — always parameterize your generics and treat unchecked warnings as compilation errors.
